title: Detection of Search Open Technical Databases
shortTitle: Detection of Search Open Technical Databases
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary queries against public technical databases, including domain name registration records, passive domain name system history, certificate transparency logs, internet scan results and breach collections. These sources let an attacker rebuild your infrastructure picture without sending a single packet to your network, which makes the collection phase invisible to ordinary monitoring. The telemetry that helps is monitoring of your own registration and name server records, certificate transparency feeds, passive resolution history and deception services on retired addresses. It fails in practice because the queries are made against third party services, so the defender usually sees a change in the database rather than the person who read it.

beginner.definition: A technical database holds facts about the internet. It may list domain owners, mail servers or certificates. Many of these databases are public. An attacker reads them to build a picture of your systems. This detection watches your own entries in those databases for changes and for signs of interest.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot see a stranger reading a public register, but you can watch the register. That is the idea behind this detection. When your domain records, mail servers or certificates change, an attacker can see it too. This often happens before your own team notices. A new certificate may reveal an internal name that was never meant to be public. An old record may still point to a system you retired, and an attacker can claim that name. Watching these sources closes a gap that network monitoring cannot reach.
howItWorks: A monitoring service collects every new certificate issued for names that belong to your organisation.
The same service records changes to domain registration data and to name server entries.
A passive domain name system feed shows which names resolve and where they point over time.
The detection compares each new record with your approved inventory of public names.
An unknown name, a changed mail server or a certificate for a retired subdomain raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a public notice board in a town square. Anyone may pin a note and anyone may read the board. A shopkeeper checks the board each morning to see if somebody has pinned a notice about his shop. He cannot stop people reading it, but he can correct a false notice quickly. Your domain records and certificates sit on that board. Your detection is the morning check. It does not catch the reader. It tells you the moment your public facts change, before somebody acts on them.
takeaways: Public registers change constantly, and attackers read them before you do.
Certificate transparency reveals internal names you did not mean to publish.
An inventory of approved public names makes changes easy to spot.

objectives: Name the public technical databases an attacker uses during reconnaissance.
Explain what certificate transparency logs reveal about your domains.
Describe how to watch registration and name server records for changes.
Compare new public records with an approved inventory of names.
Prioritise removals when an internal name appears in public data.
dataSources: Certificate transparency log monitors filtered to names in your registered domain list
Domain registration and name server record change monitoring for your registered domains
Passive domain name system resolution history for your public names and address ranges
Internal inventory of approved public names, addresses and certificate purposes
Deception service logs on retired public addresses and subdomains that should be silent
logic: The pattern is a change in the public technical record of your organisation that was not produced by an approved process, such as a new certificate for an internal sounding name, a changed mail exchanger record or a registration detail update. The fields to correlate are the record name, the record type, the value, the time of change and the approved inventory entry for that name. Benign changes come from certificate renewal automation, cloud providers that rotate endpoints and planned migrations recorded in change management. The malicious case is a record that exists in no inventory, a certificate for a name that only internal systems use, or a registration change at an hour when nobody on the team works.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Public Certificate or Domain Record Change Outside Approved Inventory
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type:
#       - 'certificate_issued'
#       - 'dns_record_change'
#       - 'registration_update'
#   filter_inventory:
#     record_name|in: 'approved_public_names'
#   filter_automated_renewal:
#     issuer|contains: 'automated_renewal_account'
#   condition: selection and not filter_inventory and not filter_automated_renewal
# level: low
falsePositives: Automated certificate renewal pipelines that use a new issuing account.
Cloud providers that rotate service endpoints and update name server records.
A marketing campaign that publishes a new subdomain before the inventory is updated.
A domain registrar that changes its own contact or billing records on your behalf.
tuningNotes: Keep the approved name inventory connected to your change process, so that a planned migration does not raise an alert. Filter the automated certificate renewal accounts you use and the name servers of your domain provider. Scope the rule to your registered domains and to names that contain internal words. If you narrow the rule to internal sounding names only, you lose the ability to spot a look alike domain registered by somebody else, so keep a separate watch on similar names and review that list weekly rather than in real time.
